title: Edge latency vs quality sweep: kernel profiles and notes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures the experimental sweep we ran to map perceived quality (basic LM metrics + human-lite checks) against per-request latency on small-batch/edge-like conditions. Goal: actionable guidance for kernel/runtime patches that improve p50/p95 latency without regressing perceived output quality when using lower-precision model variants (INT8/AWQ/GPTQ/FP8).

Background / motivation:
- Product context: many customers run latency-sensitive endpoints with batch size 1 and tight SLOs (~50–150ms end-to-end for short prompts).
- Typical lever space: choose precision (FP16/FP8/INT8/GPTQ/AWQ), choose kernel implementation (fused vs split GEMM, attention kernel variants), enable caching/prefetch, and configure microbatching heuristics.
- Hypothesis: some kernel variants offer wins for batch=1 tail latency at small sequence lengths but lead to small quality regressions; we want to quantify where the break-even points are.

Experimental setup (summary):
- Runtime: redwood-runtime v0.9.2 (local patch branch: perf/edge-launch-fix)
- Hardware: H100-80GB (driver 535.86), A100-80GB (driver 515.48), T4 (for practical edge comparison)
- CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN: CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS 12.0, cuDNN 9.3
- Models: distilled-{gpt-like}-small (0.6B), redwood-mini-1.3B, redwood-3B-ref (GPT2-ish architecture used for controlled eval)
- Precision variants: FP16 baseline, FP8 (E4M2-like profile), INT8 post-training (per-channel quant on weight), GPTQ (128Kiters), AWQ (mixed-group quant)
- Kernels evaluated: fused-gemm (single kernel for QKV + projection), split-gemm (two kernels), attention-fused (one-pass rotary+softmax), attention-split (separate kernels), custom-kernel-low-lat (SM-level tiling tuned for small M/K ratios)
- Workloads: short prompts (8–64 tokens) produced to generate 16–128 tokens of output per request; both single-turn and chat-type multi-part prompts
- Profilers: nsight-cuProfiler for micro-GPU traces, custom tracing in runtime (per-kernel timing hooks), py-spy for Python overhead, and device-side time stamps (cudaEventElapsed)
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 token latency, total end-to-end request latency (ms), tokens/sec (throughput), static quality: perplexity on heldout slices, dynamic quality: 200 prompt manual spot checks for hallucination/fluency tagged by two annotators; MRR on a small rerank eval

Run matrix (selected axes):
- Batch size: 1 only (emphasis on latency SLO), sometimes batch=2 for comparison
- Seq length: 16/32/64 context; generation length: 32 tokens
- Kernel x precision x hw x model combinations ~ 240 runs; each run warmup 10 requests, measured over 200 requests

Key findings (high level):
1) Per-kernel launch overhead dominates at batch=1 for small matmuls: split-gemm implementations had measurable +12–25% p99 compared to fused counterparts on H100 for 1.3B and 3B models. The main cause is per-kernel launch + global memory synchronization spikes.
2) INT8 post-training sometimes reduces token compute time by 25–40% on T4 and A100 when GEMM shapes are large, but for small heads/short seqs the quantized kernels lost advantage due to additional dequant/ requant passes added in the runtime. Net: INT8 benefit appears only when combined with fused kernels and when sequence length >= 32.
3) AWQ/GPTQ variants: AWQ with group-size=32 delivered near-INT8 latency but with higher quality than naive PTQ INT8 on our Q-tableau (perplexity delta ~ +3% vs FP16). GPTQ gave best quality but had slightly higher kernel latency due to extra packing/unpacking code paths in our patched runtime.
4) FP8: FP8 kernels reduced compute latency comparable to INT8 on H100 but introduced occasional numerical spikes (observed as p99 latency jitter and one model-run divergence) — these correlate with softmax exponent range expansions; mitigating strategy: small-fp8-scaling clamps in attention softmax stabilizes runs.
5) Attention kernels are where quality-sensitive regressions appear: replacing fused attention with split attention plus int8+requant caused top-k token probability mass shifts — explains human-flagged fluency hits.

Representative numbers (redwood-mini-1.3B, H100, seq=32, gen=32, batch=1):
- FP16 + fused: p50=28ms, p95=42ms, p99=58ms, perplexity=14.8
- INT8 (PTQ) + fused: p50=20ms, p95=32ms, p99=55ms, perplexity=16.1
- AWQ (group32) + fused: p50=22ms, p95=34ms, p99=48ms, perplexity=15.2
- FP8 + fused (clamp): p50=18ms, p95=28ms, p99=50ms, perplexity=15.8
Notes: numbers are median across 5 runs; p99 sensitivity to background noise (other tenants) was observed and so we ran isolated experiments too.

Profiling observations / bottlenecks:
- Kernel launch & small GEMM inefficiency: on H100 the overhead is lower than A100 but still visible. Reducing number of kernels (fused ops) yields consistent wins.
- Memory bandwidth: INT8/FP8 reduced memory transfer size but dequant/quant overhead in host code added CPU overhead and extra memcpy calls in our runtime.
- Kernel packing/unpacking: GPTQ/AWQ sometimes require on-the-fly reordering; the current implementation does this on CPU which causes blocking stalls. Offloading pack/unpack to GPU or reusing prepacked buffers reduces observed p99 by ~15%.
- Attention softmax numerical edge cases: FP8 needs dynamic scaling; without clamps some tokens produce extreme exps causing expensive reductions and tail CPU path.
- KV cache interaction: cache read/write patterns when using quantized keys resulted in extra conversions; caching prequantized KV (and keeping them on GPU) reduces both latency and jitter.

Quick patches tried during sweep (and impact):
- prepack-gemm-on-load: prepack weight matrices into kernel-friendly layout at model load time (costs ~120ms at load) -> reduced per-request compute by 6–12% for quant kernels.
- gpu-pack-unpack: moved packing for GPTQ->GPU via small CUDA kernels -> reduced blocking CPU stalls; p95 improved ~14% on A100.
- fp8-softmax-clamp: add clamp to exp inputs -> removed rare numerical divergence and reduced p99 jitter by ~20% in FP8 runs.
- kernel-launch-batching: coalesce small kernel launches into a single kernel with sequential logic where possible -> p99 reduced but increased code complexity; won for 1.3B, more work needed for 3B+.

Qualitative check (annotator notes):
- INT8 PTQ: more factual mistakes on long-tail knowledge prompts; common failure mode: fused attention missing small-scale precision in logits leading to altered argmaxes.
- AWQ: generally maintained coherence; occasional tokenization-level artifacts on very short prompts (2–4 tokens) observed.
- GPTQ: minimal visible regressions in the manual set, consistent with small perplexity lift.

Recommendations (near-term):
1) Prioritize fused kernels for small-batch/edge path — reduce kernel count per token.
2) Move pack/unpack to GPU or prepack at load time for quant variants (apply to AWQ/GPTQ paths).
3) Introduce FP8 softmax clamps and conservative scaling heuristics as runtime defaults behind an opt-in flag.
4) Provide model-precision guidance matrix for customers: for seq<=16 recommend FP16/fused or FP8-clamped; for seq>=32 recommend AWQ+prepacked or INT8+fused depending on quality targets.
5) Add a microbenchmark harness that runs the exact RPC path (including network and serialization) to capture real end-to-end SLOs — current runs are local and slightly optimistic.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Group size sensitivity for AWQ: we tested 32/64; intermediate sizes and adaptive group-size per-layer might yield better quality/latency Pareto frontier.
- Pre-packing memory cost vs latency tradeoff across model sizes and deployment density. How much extra GPU RAM can Dedicated/Private customers tolerate?
- Should we expose an "edge-precision" profile in the API that picks FP8-clamped or AWQ depending on model size/seq?

Appendix: selected commands and notes
- micro-run (example): 
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python perf_run.py --model redwood-mini-1.3B --precision awq --batch 1 --seq 32 --gen 32 --warmup 10 --iters 200 --kernels fused
- trace collection: nsight-cuProfiler CLI, then convert to timeline with our trace->json tool (trace2timeline)
- packing patch: see PR #412 (gpu pack small kernels)

Notes to implementer: this is a working doc. Some data points (especially p99) vary with cluster noise; re-run on isolated infra before shipping guidance to product. Prioritize small, low-risk runtime changes (fp8 clamp, prepack) for the next release.

Contact: Anika Rao (eng-serving-runtime) — slack @anika; filing follow-up RFC against runtime/ops for prepack strategy.
